AI co-authorship attributed in commits/PRs
Small, focused PRs that are easy to review

Onboarding / “how this repo works” entry point

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture is deterministically fixed at 49/100 (exposure unrated — dependencies weren't inspected). report.headline: LeRobot runs a mature, CI-gated engineering process with genuinely useful agent-guidance docs, but AI-native adoption still looks more like infrastructure-in-place than habit-in-practice — placing the org at the top of L3 Augmented, with security-automation and AI-verification gaps standing between it and L4.
strengths: Deep, current agent guidance (CLAUDE.md + AGENTS.md + a separate AGENT_GUIDE.md) with real commands and an accurate architecture map, not boilerplate
Comprehensive CI/CD: 14 workflows spanning lint/test/build/deploy with required status checks and policy-as-code
A large, healthy test suite (252 files, 0.47 ratio) backing fast, small-batch merges (65% small PRs, 4.3h median time-to-merge)
Explicit AI-contribution governance signal — CONTRIBUTING.md points to a dedicated AI_POLICY.md, not just a generic code-of-conduct
Responsive maintainer engagement (0.3h median time-to-first-review) suggesting an actively steered, not just automated, process
risks: Supply-chain automation is thin for a widely-depended-on library: no SAST, no dependency-update bot, no signed releases/SBOM, and under half of CI Action refs pinned by SHA
AI involvement in actual PR authorship is minimal (3%), so the sophisticated agent docs may not yet reflect how most contributors actually work
Review coverage on merged PRs is only 40% despite a branch-protection rule requiring approval, implying a meaningful share of changes get lighter human scrutiny than the rule implies

No structured evals/golden-test harness exists to verify AI-generated changes before merge — a gap that matters more as a robotics library where incorrect policy/control code has physical consequences
Two CI workflows grant broad write permissions, widening the blast radius if any workflow or its dependencies were compromised

roadmap.title: AI review/automation bots run in CI, but it's unclear whether they can act — or only advise

roadmap.title: AI governance exists on paper (AI_POLICY.md) but no visible harness verifies AI-authored changes before merge

report.headline: Transformers has some of the deepest, most enforceable AI-agent guidance in open source and a massive automated test suite, but the org has deliberately kept agentic autonomy on a short leash — merge gates, AI-review harnesses, and release-integrity controls remain thin relative to both its scale and the volume of AI-assisted contribution pressure it already absorbs.
strengths: Four converging, technique-rich agent-guidance files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .ai/AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md) built around a real, enforceable Mandatory Agentic contribution policy
An exceptional automated test suite (1,647 files, 0.54 test-to-source ratio) with coverage tracking and a deliberate slow/fast test-tiering philosophy
Strong CI security hygiene: 100% permission-scoped workflows, 100% SHA-pinned actions, SAST on every PR, and a security policy with model-specific risk guidance
Fast, small-batch human delivery cadence (median 1.5h to merge, 90% small PRs) showing a well-oiled contribution pipeline
risks: Branch protection is nominal — 0 required approvals and no required status checks on the default branch — so nothing structurally stops an unreviewed or CI-failing change (human or AI-authored) from merging
A critical dangerous-workflow pattern (assign-reviewers.yml checking out code on pull_request_target) creates a real code-execution exposure from untrusted PRs
No evals/golden-test harness exists to verify AI-generated changes before human review, and CONTRIBUTING.md already signals maintainer review capacity is overwhelmed by agent-authored PRs
No artifact signing, provenance, or SBOM generation, leaving release integrity unverifiable for one of the most widely-depended-upon ML libraries in existence
A wide gap between AI-governance depth (a mandatory, detailed contribution policy) and measured practice (only 3% of PRs show AI involvement, only 50% of merged PRs get an approving review)

roadmap.title: Branch protection is switched on but enforces almost nothing underneath it
roadmap.rationale: The default branch is marked protected, but 0 approvals and no status checks are actually required, so the extensive CI (57 workflows, lint, type-checking, tests) currently functions as advisory signal rather than a structural gate on what merges — for both human and AI-authored changes.
explore: What would change if at least one required status check (tests or make style) were added to the default branch's protection rules?
Is the current 0-approval setting a deliberate trust model for a small set of maintainers, or has it just never been revisited?

roadmap.title: A workflow pattern gives untrusted PR code a path into a privileged context
roadmap.rationale: assign-reviewers.yml checks out code on pull_request_target, a well-known pattern for privilege escalation from fork PRs since that event runs with elevated token scope against attacker-controlled code — as AI-assisted and external PR volume grows, so does exposure through this specific path.
explore: Does assign-reviewers.yml actually need a full checkout, or could it operate on the event payload alone?
Would splitting the trusted (label/assign) logic from any untrusted-code-dependent logic close this gap without losing functionality?

roadmap.title: AI-assisted contributions are governed defensively but not yet verified by a harness
roadmap.rationale: The Mandatory Agentic contribution policy is effective at deterring low-value or duplicate agent PRs, but there's no evidence of an evals/golden-test harness that verifies AI-produced changes before a human ever looks — CONTRIBUTING.md already flags that maintainer review bandwidth is being overwhelmed by agent-written PRs and comments.
explore: Could a lightweight automated pre-check (e.g., confirming a PR only touches what it claims, or passes make check-repo) triage agent PRs before human attention is spent?
Is there appetite for a small golden-test set that specifically exercises AI-authored model code before it reaches a reviewer?

roadmap.title: Review participation runs well below contribution volume and velocity
roadmap.rationale: Only half of merged PRs analyzed carried an approving review (averaging 0.2 reviews per PR), while merges happen quickly (median 1.5h) — a high-trust, high-velocity model that may not hold up as AI-assisted PR volume increases further.
explore: Is the current review rate a conscious trust model for maintainer self-merges on small changes, or a capacity symptom worth naming?
Would making review-rate a visible, tracked metric change how the team thinks about the trade-off between speed and review coverage?

roadmap.title: Released artifacts carry no signature or SBOM
roadmap.rationale: As one of the most widely depended-upon ML libraries, unsigned releases and the absence of an SBOM mean downstream consumers have no way to verify provenance — a gap that matters more, not less, as AI-driven supply chains face growing scrutiny.
explore: Would cosign/SLSA-style provenance be feasible to bolt onto the existing PyPI release pipeline?
Is there downstream demand (enterprise users, compliance requirements) that would make SBOM generation worth prioritizing now versus later?

discrepancies.claim: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md explicitly document `make typing` running the `ty` type checker as a mandatory pre-PR step, yet D6's signal list credits only a linter, formatter, and PR template — type-checking enforcement appears undercounted.

AGENTS.md states that 'hosted review agents should discover this guidance from the committed root AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md files,' implying an AI PR-review process is part of the standard workflow, yet D4's score of 25 credits only issue/PR automation and a dependency bot, suggesting agentic review-workflow presence may be undercounted (though no specific bot workflow file was directly sampled to confirm this).
